name: inversion-of-control
intent: Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour.
problem: A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.
context: Applies wherever generic flow logic has to be specialised by application code: UI toolkits and event loops that decide when handlers fire, server containers and engines that own request dispatch and component lifecycle, test runners that own fixture and test sequencing, plugin hosts, and effect runtimes that own program entry. It is the defining characteristic of a framework as opposed to a library (a library is called by your code; a framework calls your code), and it usually arrives bundled with a container, dispatcher or engine - what remains to design is where the boundary sits and how much lifecycle you hand over.
benefits: Reuse of the generic flow: the framework's sequencing logic is written and tested once and specialised per application instead of being re-implemented in every caller (Johnson & Foote's 'extensible skeletons').

Extension without modification: new behaviour arrives through hook implementations, registrations or plugins rather than edits inside the framework - the open/closed principle applied to control flow.

Independent evolution: both sides depend only on the extension contract, so framework and application can be developed, versioned and deployed separately (the compile-time dependency direction is inverted along with the calls).

Uniform policy at the hook boundary: lifecycle setup, transactions, security checks, scheduling and resource management are applied once by the owner of the flow instead of being repeated by every extension.

Deferred implementation choice: which implementation fills a hook can be decided at assembly or deployment time, enabling configuration-specific variants and test doubles without touching the framework.
Framework and hooks are separately testable: the skeleton can be exercised with stub hooks, and hooks can be exercised by driving them the way the framework does.
tradeoffs: Inverted call flow is harder to read and debug: entry points are not called from visible application code, so stack traces begin inside framework internals and 'who calls this, and when' must be learned from documentation (Fowler notes that inversion of control 'tends to be hard to understand and leads to problems when you are trying to debug').
Framework lock-in: hook signatures, annotation semantics and lifecycle guarantees are framework-specific, so application code written against one container or toolkit is costly to move to another.

Implicit lifecycle and hidden ordering: the framework decides when hooks run (startup order, shutdown, cancellation, re-entrancy), which produces surprising initialisation order and callbacks that fire after their object was disposed.

The inverted side is harder to test directly: a hook that passes when called in a unit test may behave differently under the framework's calling protocol, so tests must simulate the container, loop or dispatcher.
Overhead moves into code you do not control: container scanning and reflection, per-event virtual dispatch and callback allocation are paid on paths the application cannot easily optimise.
Failure semantics belong to the framework: exceptions thrown from a hook may be swallowed, retried or converted by the loop, so a broken hook can fail silently unless the contract says otherwise.
With a single implementation and a single call site, the skeleton plus registration machinery is pure indirection compared with the direct call it replaces.

participants.responsibility: Owns the call flow (main loop, lifecycle, request or message dispatch) and defines the extension points at which application code is invoked; it plays the role of the main program.
The abstraction - abstract class, interface, protocol, trait or callback signature - that application code implements or supplies; it is the boundary across which control is inverted.
Implements the contract and reacts when the framework calls it; it decides what happens at a hook but never when the hook runs.
Tells the framework which implementation to call and when - subclassing, an explicit registration call, decorator or annotation, configuration, or convention over names.
Decides when hooks fire (event loop, executor, container lifecycle, engine), may own the process entry point, and often manages creation, scoping and disposal of the application components.

use_cases: GUI and event-driven applications: the windowing system or runtime owns the event loop and calls your event handlers, app delegate or declarative view body.
Server-side request handling: the container, engine or router owns listen-accept-dispatch and invokes the servlets, handlers, routes or middleware you registered.
Test frameworks: the runner owns discovery, fixture setup and teardown and calls your test methods and lifecycle hooks (JUnit, pytest, xUnit).
Container-managed components: EJB, Spring, Angular or Nest components whose construction, wiring and lifecycle callbacks are driven by the container that also owns the entry point.

Plugin and extension architectures: a host defines extension points and third-party plugins implement them, with the host deciding when each plugin is consulted (IDEs, browsers, build tools, game engines).
Inverted program entry: effect runtimes and app frameworks where the runtime's main calls the run value or app structure you provide instead of you orchestrating from main.
Callback-based C APIs: a library call such as qsort or a GLib main loop calls your function pointer per element or event - a small-scale realization of the same inversion.

Cloud Functions-as-a-Service: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions own the request dispatch and cold-start lifecycle; your handler is a hook called by the platform, making serverless a live deployment of the Hollywood principle.

Reactive streams and event-driven pipelines: frameworks like Reactor, RxJava, or Node.js EventEmitter own the subscription and back-pressure loop; operators and subscribers are hooks that the runtime calls on data availability.

Microservices sidecar and service mesh: an Envoy or Linkerd proxy sidecar owns the connection lifecycle and calls application code through a defined protocol; the application registers health checks and request handlers as IoC hooks.

Orleans virtual actor model: the Orleans runtime owns the grain lifecycle, activation and deactivation, and calls grain methods as directed by the scheduler; grain code is a hook implementation invoked by the framework.

ASP.NET Core middleware: the host builds the request pipeline and invokes each registered RequestDelegate in order; middleware can run before and after the next delegate or short-circuit, so the application supplies components while the server owns request dispatch.

JUnit Jupiter extension model: the JUnit engine discovers tests and invokes registered Before*/After* lifecycle callbacks around user test methods; extensions customize execution without owning when tests run.

Kubernetes controllers: the controller manager owns reconciliation loops that watch API state and repeatedly invokes controller reconciliation logic to converge current state on desired state; controllers supply behavior while Kubernetes schedules dispatch.
avoid_when: One implementation, one call site and no extension points: a direct call sequence is clearer, faster and easier to debug than a framework skeleton plus registration.
The application must control call timing itself (batch jobs, scripts, latency-critical pipelines): explicit orchestration beats inversion that cannot be seen in the code.

The surrounding stack already inverts the flow (web framework, UI toolkit, executor) and you would only be adding hooks inside hooks - use the existing extension points instead of building a second framework.
The team cannot absorb the framework's implicit lifecycle: hidden initialisation order and callback semantics then cause more defects than the decoupling removes.
The 'framework' would be a thin wrapper around a single function - the registration and lifecycle machinery costs more than the code it organises.
anti_patterns: 'IoC container' relabelling: calling any dependency-injection container usage 'inversion of control' and introducing a container where passing a dependency into a constructor would do (DI is about wiring, IoC is about who initiates the call).
Framework for one caller: an abstract skeleton with a hook registry that has exactly one implementation, forcing readers to reconstruct a control flow a direct call would have shown.
God template method: a base class that calls a long fixed sequence of hooks, recreating a rigid pipeline nobody can safely extend so that the framework becomes the thing everyone must modify.
Callbacks without ownership: listeners registered with no unregistration or lifecycle binding, so callbacks outlive their objects and touch disposed state.
Configuration-only control flow: wiring call targets solely through annotations or external configuration, so no static reference shows what actually runs.
design_principles: Hollywood principle: the framework decides when your code runs, while your code decides only what it does.
Dependency inversion: the framework depends on the abstraction (the hook contract) and application code depends on that same abstraction, not on framework internals.
Open/closed principle: the generic flow stays closed for modification while new behaviour is added through extension points.
Separation of concerns: invariant sequencing stays in the framework and only the varying behaviour lives in the application.
Single responsibility: the framework owns lifecycle and dispatch; each hook owns one step of behaviour.
Interface segregation: an extension point should expose only the hooks its extensions need (role interfaces) rather than one all-purpose extension interface.
best_practices: Document the calling contract: which hooks the framework calls, in what order, on which thread, with which lifecycle, re-entrancy, failure and cancellation guarantees.
Keep hook contracts narrow and typed, and let the framework depend only on the abstraction, never on concrete extensions.
Give every registration an owner and a deterministic end: bind callbacks to their object's lifecycle and unregister or dispose them explicitly.
Define failure semantics - whether an exception from a hook fails the request, is logged and swallowed, or is retried - instead of leaving it to the loop.
Keep hooks thin: delegate to plain objects that know nothing about the framework (the humble-object style) so behaviour stays unit-testable.
Choose the smallest inversion that solves the problem: one callback registration or interface implementation often beats an annotation-driven container.
Design hooks for concurrent or re-entrant invocation: assume the framework may call them from any thread and more than once.

Profile hook contracts against real dispatch before committing: write a behavioural test that calls your hook the way the framework will, before the framework exists; this catches missing state and wrong signatures early.

Validate container or registry configuration at startup, not lazily: resolve every registered singleton eagerly to catch missing implementations, circular dependencies and override chains before the first request.
Distinguish singleton scope from global state: a singleton component managed by the IoC container is scoped to the container, not to the process; design it to be disposable and testable in isolation.
Name lifecycle semantics in the implementation name: a class named 'UserService' versus 'RequestUserService' should make the re-entrancy and scoping contract immediately legible to readers.

Avoid ambient contexts and static service locators as an escape hatch: they make dependencies implicit, complicate testing, and hide the true coupling surface; prefer constructor injection even when it is verbose.

Treat the composition root as the only place where the container is referenced in application code: no container-aware application code above the composition root; this keeps the architecture testable and portable.
sources: Ralph E. Johnson and Brian Foote, Designing Reusable Classes, Journal of Object-Oriented Programming 1(2), 1988 - the paper that introduced the term: the framework calls the user-supplied methods and 'inversion of control gives frameworks the power to serve as extensible skeletons'; http://www.laputan.org/drc/drc.html
Martin Fowler, Inversion of Control (bliki, 2005) - the Hollywood Principle and the framework-versus-library distinction; https://martinfowler.com/bliki/InversionOfControl.html

Martin Fowler, Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection Pattern (2004) - separates control inversion over call flow from dependency assembly; https://martinfowler.com/articles/injection.html
Brett L. Schuchert, DIP in the Wild (martinfowler.com) - 'DI is about wiring, IoC is about direction, and DIP is about shape'; https://martinfowler.com/articles/dipInTheWild.html

Stefan Sobernig and Uwe Zdun, Inversion-of-Control Layer, EuroPLoP '10 (Proceedings of the 15th European Conference on Pattern Languages of Programs, ACM) - the pattern in its architectural dimension; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2328909.2328935 and https://eprints.cs.univie.ac.at/2822/1/Inversion-of-Control_Layer.pdf

Alistair Cockburn, Discussion of Dependency Inversion, Dependency Injection, Dependency Lookup, Configurable Receiver and Inversion of Control - IoC as the two-step registration-then-callback mechanism; https://alistaircockburn.com/Discussion%20of%20dependency%20inversion%20etc.pdf
Inversion of control (Wikipedia) - the framework-calls-back definition and the separate 'IoC container' sense; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_of_control

Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, 2002 - the canonical reference for enterprise developers on framework-call-back structure, Separated Interface, and DI/IoC distinctions in enterprise systems; https://martinfowler.com/books/eaa.html

Steven van Deursen and Mark Seemann, Dependency Injection: Principles, Practices, and Patterns, 2019 - definitive modern book separating DI from IoC containers; introduces the Composition Root pattern, analyzes constructor vs setter vs ambient context injection across Java, C#, Python, Ruby; https://www.manning.com/books/dependency-injection-principles-practices-and-patterns

Erich Gamma, Design Patterns for Object-Oriented Framework Development, 1994 - describes IoC as the structural foundation of frameworks: hook methods, template-method and factory-method as concrete mechanisms for inverting call direction in frameworks; https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.56.7986

Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), Clean Architecture — A Craftsman's Guide to Software Structure, 2017 - argues that the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) is the essential rule for architecture; connects DIP to IoC as the structural mechanism for plugin architectures and framework boundaries; https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/clean-architecture-a/9780134494272/

Spring Framework Documentation, Component Patterns in the Spring Framework — Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection, 2024 - Spring's official documentation distinguishing the IoC container (bean factory) from DI wiring semantics; covers annotation-driven, XML, and JavaConfig registration models; https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/core/beans.html

Angular Team, Google, Angular Dependency Injection — The Official Guide, 2024 - Angular's hierarchical injectors mirror the component tree; opaque-token system implements Separated Interface in TypeScript; canonical modern IoC implementation for SPA frameworks; https://angular.io/guide/dependency-injection
Ralph E. Johnson and Brian Foote, Designing Reusable Classes (1988) - canonical origin and extensible-skeleton framing; https://www.laputan.org/drc.html

ASP.NET Core middleware documentation - official request-pipeline docs showing the host invokes registered middleware and controls continuation or short-circuiting; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/?view=aspnetcore-10.0
JUnit User Guide, Test Lifecycle Callbacks - official extension callbacks invoked by the JUnit engine around user test execution; https://docs.junit.org/6.2.0/extensions/test-lifecycle-callbacks.html

Kubernetes documentation, Controllers - official reconciliation-loop description where controller runtime observes state and drives convergence; https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/controller/

Mark Seemann, Service Locator: roles vs. mechanics - critique of using a DI container as a runtime service locator and guidance on composition-root boundaries; https://blog.ploeh.dk/2011/08/25/ServiceLocatorrolesvs.mechanics/
